title: Unified backoff, idempotency semantics, and hedged-request telemetry for global failover
creator: Priya Patel
description: Problem statement: We lack a single interoperable contract for retries, backoff shapes, idempotency key semantics, and hedged request orchestration across services and SDKs. This leads to inconsistent behaviour during multi-region failovers, duplicated work in application code, and unclear telemetry for SLO-driven load shedding decisions. Goal: deliver a cross-service standard and SDKs' compatible implementation that unifies: 1) Retry/timeout/backoff profiles (SLO-class mapping), 2) Idempotency header format and server-side enforcement expectations, 3) Hedged request orchestration and response arbitration, 4) Circuit-breaker and load-shed interplay, and 5) telemetry and traces to measure cost, waste, and correctness.
acceptance_criteria:
- Single spec document published and approved by SE/Platform leads.
- Server-side support for new idempotency header X-RW-Idempotency with 3 supported modes (required, optional, disabled) behind feature flag.
- SDKs (Go, Python, Node) expose a unified RetryPolicy object that maps to 'slo-class' (low-latency, standard, throughput) and implements exponential + jitter backoff defaults from the spec.
- Hedged request protocol implemented as an opt-in parameter (max_hedges, hedge_delay_ms) with deterministic arbitration: earliest-success wins, later responses dropped and accounted in telemetry.
- Circuit breaker metadata propagated via headers for coordinated shedding (X-RW-Circuit-Version).
- Dashboards updated with new metrics: rw.retries.count, rw.hedges.count, rw.hedges.waste_tokens, rw.idempotency.conflicts, rw.backoff.latency-p95.
- Migration plan and rollout playbook document with canary steps and rollback criteria.
proposal_summary: We propose a pragmatic spec that balances safety and developer ergonomics: - Default retry behavior is conservative and SLO-aware: low-latency SLOs get small retry windows and brittle hedging; throughput SLOs get larger windows and stronger hedging. - Idempotency keys are normalized: 128-bit UUID v4 or base64-encoded client nonce; servers must return 409 with specific error code when mismatched semantics detected. - Hedging: controller issues a second request after hedge_delay_ms; SDKs should support bounded hedges and expose the hedge_id for tracing. - Circuit breakers communicate reason codes and version header so downstream routers can coordinate shedding decisions rather than blind drops. - Telemetry must correlate hedges with cost impact so Optimize can recommend knob changes.
implementation_notes: Server-side: introduce IdempotencyStore v2 that supports TTL, dedupe window, and conflict resolution policies. Add middleware to runtime to honor X-RW-Idempotency semantics. SDK: Add RetryPolicy and HedgingOptions classes; use common algorithm placed in shared lib (go/py/node). Router: when in multi-region failover mode, use slo-class -> region-preference mapping and consult circuit-version header for coordinated shedding. Observability: emit span tags (rw.hedge=true, rw.idempotency=hit/miss/conflict). Add a 'waste_tokens' counter that sums tokens used by hedged requests that did not win arbitration.
tradeoffs_and_risks:
- Strong idempotency enforcement can break some legacy clients; mitigate via opt-in header modes and a compatibility migration window.
- Hedging increases cost; aim to make it explicit opt-in per endpoint and measure waste_tokens to justify.
- Coordinated shedding requires small header surface area between services; risk of coupling microservices — mitigate via versioned headers and backward compatibility.
- Precise arbitration across regions increases complexity (clock skew, duplicate responses); rely on request arrival ordering and explicit hedge_id rather than clocks.
rollout_plan: Phase 0 (two weeks): publish spec and tests; implement server-side feature-flagged support in two non-critical services. Phase 1 (four weeks): ship SDK changes behind opt-in flags, run integration tests with canary traffic (10% of traffic) to measure retry/hedge metrics. Phase 2 (three weeks): enable on additional services with traffic shaping and add dashboards. Phase 3: default enablement on low-risk endpoints and provide migration guidance for high-risk/legacy endpoints. Each phase includes a rollback window and SLO guardrails (error rate > 0.5% or cost increase > 20% triggers rollback).
testing_and_validation:
- Unit tests for RetryPolicy permutations and hedge arbitration.
- Integration test harness (k6) simulating region outage and measuring p50/p95, retries per request, and hedged success ratio.
- Chaos experiment: induce 150ms added latency in primary region and ensure failover + hedging behaviour conforms to SLO mapping.
- Load test to quantify waste_tokens under different hedge_delay_ms settings.
- Security review to ensure idempotency header can't be abused for replay attacks; integrate with KMS for signing optional idempotency keys.
migration_steps: 1) Add support for X-RW-Idempotency with mode 'optional' on servers; SDKs default to 'optional'. 2) Enable detailed telemetry for 2 weeks to discover endpoints with frequent idempotency conflicts. 3) Reach out to internal consumers to migrate to idempotent design for state-modifying endpoints. 4) Flip to 'required' for new endpoints only. 5) Provide compatibility shim for legacy clients.
open_questions:
- Should hedge arbitration be 'first-response-wins' globally or scoped to region affinity? (Trade-off: deterministic but may favor proximity.)
- What is the canonical idempotency key format for large bodies where clients reuse keys? (UUID v4 vs HMAC-signed nonce)
- Acceptable default for max_hedges for low-latency vs throughput endpoints?
- Do we require servers to persist idempotency results for full TTL or allow eventual storage for lower-cost endpoints?
